utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff. Can you see if you can get through this in 40 minutes --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- and that will then be three hours in all.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, before the break, we had started to speak about personnel from the Serbian state security in the region. And you have already mentioned Radoslav Kostic being there. And in your statement you mentioned Branko Glusica. Where was he situated within the region? Where was his office?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're not getting a translation of that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear the English on this channel?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Try again.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can you repeat your answer. We didn't get any translation of your answer. Where was Mr. Glusica sitting?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For a while, it was in Dalj, and then in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We're switching to another channel, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And did he share an office? Did he share an office with another official from your region?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did, with the chief of SUP in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You have mentioned in your statement a certain Lemic, alias Milan Lakic. What dealings did you have with him?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lemic was in the area of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, and he was in the negotiating team, mine, when we negotiated with the Croats, or rather, the Erdut agreement, when it was signed.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How did he get into your team? Did you select him or did someone else decide that he should be on the team?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly, but yes, he was a member of the team at any rate.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Those personnel -- those members from the Serbian DB, to whom did they report? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You have described the power structure in the region, mentioning the JNA and its power and then the shift of power when Badza arrived. In the power structure in the region in Slavonia, Baranja, Western Srem, what was the position of the personnel of the Serbian DB?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The Serbian DB personnel, what was its position in regard to power, influence?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A great deal of influence.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I will now talk with you about the -- your own meetings with Mr. Milosevic. And we have to -- you have described this here in the courtroom and we cannot refer to your previous statement. When did you meet Mr. Milosevic for the first time and what was the purpose of the meeting? You do not need to find it in your statement, Mr. Milanovic. Just as you remember it.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I met Mr. Milosevic for the first time in 1993 and 1994. The object of the meeting was going to -- the representatives of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem going to his cabinet, his offices. Goran Hadzic led the delegation. I can't remember exactly what it was that we discussed on that first meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you see Mr. Milosevic in relation to the Vance Plan at some point in time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did go.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you recall when that was?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a little earlier on. It was a large delegation, and the topic of discussion was acceptance of the Vance Owen Plan and preparations for the arrival of the international community to the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you meet Mr. Milosevic in a delegation in relation to the elections in the RSK?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And what was -- did Mr. Milosevic request anything of you and the delegation at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the topic of the meeting were elections in Republika Srpska Krajina, and the subject was who the president would be. And Mr. Milosevic at the time placed Mr. Milan Maric in the forefront, in relation to the others.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And what about Mr. Hadzic? Did he become a candidate, and what was Mr. Milosevic's position as to that fact?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Milan Martic, with a "T."

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, it was Mr. Milosevic's position that Goran Hadzic should not be a candidate, but nonetheless he was a candidate. However, at the elections, Mr. Martic won.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did Mr. Martic win in the first round? Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He won in the second round of the elections, and the opposite candidate was Milan Babic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And in the first round, when Mr. Hadzic took part as a candidate, did that cause any friction between you and the Serbian MUP and others you were related to?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was tension, because in the first round I did not lend my support to Milan Martic, and this was not seen as being the thing to do. In the second round, Radovan Stojicic, Badza, prevailed upon me, to influence me to help, and Martic won.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You have described your activities as head of the negotiation team in 1995 and 1996. In this time period, did you meet Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, several times.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Would -- why would you meet him? What was the purpose of such meetings?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the subject was preparations for talks with Croatia, the Croatian side, and the international community.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Would you consult with Mr. Milosevic before you go -- you went to such negotiations and afterwards or not?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In most cases, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were suggestions made to you how to behave during the negotiations?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: More or less, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you ever act against these suggestions, or did you follow?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depended.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Can you give us an example where you did not follow?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was the question of who would be a member of the delegation, and we didn't agree on that score at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Can you -- can you describe what was requested, who should be in the delegation, and what happened?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We formed a delegation of the Srem and Baranja region for negotiations with the Croats, and Goran Hadzic was not among the members. Mr. Milosevic, however, insisted that Goran Hadzic become a member of the delegation, and that's what happened in the end.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And how did Hadzic later then during the negotiations behave Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. towards you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't really assess that now, but at first glance he was correct and proper, but I think he was working behind our backs.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When you had conversations with Mr. Milosevic, how would you address him and how would he address you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I always addressed him as "Mr. President." And he would mostly call me "Mrgud."

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were you offered a Croatian peace proposal by Ambassador Galbraith at some point in time? And what did you do?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Ambassador Galbraith did offer a proposal from the Croatian side, and in part from the international community as well. And when he came to see me that day - and the situation was complex in Krajina - Western Slavonia, and the lower half of the Knin Krajina had fallen, militarily speaking, and the possibility existed of war breaking out in the area of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem as well. And Ambassador Galbraith came to see me. He brought with him his plan or, rather, a draft plan, a proposal, and I said that I would accept it, accept reviewing it, in fact, and that I would give him an answer in a few days' time. However, I was called to Belgrade because on the RTS television station this was interpreted as me having signed an agreement already. So they called me to Belgrade the next day. Badza called me to attend a meeting with Mr. Milosevic, where the people present were the late Minister Sokolovic, Stanisic, Badza, and Mr. Milosevic himself. So I was there, and they asked me what I had done, whether I had signed anything. And I said -- I explained to them that I had signed nothing, that I had just taken the draft proposal or plan, which we would then consider and review, and then tell them that we would enter into negotiation and not outright reject it, as Martic did the Z4 plan, and the lower part of Krajina felt as a result.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You actually have --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And I will now turn to tab 27 of the Exhibit 549.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You have actually provided the agreement, the Erdut agreement. And it's at tab 27. That was finally the end result of all the negotiations. And we do not go into details, but before signing it, did you get a message from someone to do that?, to sign it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, this is a complicated issue. At the time of the signing of the agreement, the Serb delegation or Yugoslav delegation was in Dayton. I myself had entered the final stages of the negotiations because Tudjman didn't want to sign the Dayton Accords until the question of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem was solved. And on the eve of the signing, as I state in my statement, I received a message from the delegation at Dayton, which was led by Mr. Milosevic. I received this message via the assistant foreign affairs minister, Zika Jovanovic, that I should -- to the effect that I should sign the agreement, and I received that message on Friday. I explained what happened with respect to Saturday or, rather, with respect to Friday afternoon, that from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs I went to see Badza at the MUP building and that he called Dayton up and Mr. Stanisic, and Stanisic said in his message - he sent us a telegram - I can't remember the exact words, but I'll try and quote: "I've tried everything with the president, but we've lost Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. God save them." Badza answered to this message, "Don't you sign tomorrow. Let them -- let the president call me if he wants the agreement to be signed." And I said to him, "But Badza, if I don't sign tomorrow, they're going to attack on Sunday." I meant the Croats. And he was -- took the hard line and said, "Come and see me on Monday, unless I ring up to tell you otherwise." So nonetheless, in agreement with Galbraith and Stoltenberg, on Saturday I did sign the agreement, and after that they started to attack me. Mr. Milosevic's closest associates attacked me and criticised me for having done that, asking me why I did that, Kertes and all the rest, not the enumerate them all. So that would be that in brief.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And did you meet afterwards Mr. Milosevic, and what did he tell you in relation to your signing the Dayton -- the agreement, the Erdut agreement?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic told me that I had done the right thing and that was the only possible option at that point in time. And he asked me whether anybody had been attacking him [as interpreted] of his associates. I kept quiet on that score and said that nobody attacked me because I considered that that was the best line to take at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: After the Dayton -- the Erdut agreement was signed, did you continue to have meetings with Milosevic related to the implementation of the Erdut agreement?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. From time to time, I had meetings with respect to the implementation of the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And turning to tab 29 of the Exhibit 549, we have here an invitation to a meeting in Belgrade, and there is a reference made on top in handwriting, saying "for Mira from Branko." Can you tell us what that means, "for Mira from Branko"? Or rather, it's not handwriting, it's typed. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that means that this was a way of communication. The secretary of Mr. Milosevic, between her and myself. And my nickname on this occasion was Branko.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you meet in the -- in the Serbian Presidency at a location where also there was Mr. Borislav Mikelic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. And I described that in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But you have to describe it now for us. Tell us when it was and what happened.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, roughly that was after August 1995, when the lower part of Krajina fell. We had a meeting in the Presidency, and after the meeting Mr. Milosevic told me to stay behind, that he needed me for something. And at the meeting there were the representatives of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem present, because the lower part of Krajina had fallen, as I said. And among other things, the topic of discussion was -- Mikelic was -- and Mr. Milosevic spoke about him in adverse terms on that occasion. And when we left, after the meeting we went to another room, Mr. Mikelic was there, and Mr. Milosevic asked me to help him with something. I was a little taken aback, him having spoken about the man in derogatory terms at one meeting and asking me to help him at the next, and that he wanted to evict Babic from an office in Belgrade, from a commission, in fact, and have Mikelic take his place. And that was done.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Why did he ask you to do -- get involved?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know, actually. I was wondering, but probably because I was close to Badza, so he thought this would smooth the way, because otherwise Badza did not have a good attitude towards Mikelic himself.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were you asked to see Mr. Milosevic in April 1996, an occasion that ended your career in the region?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Around about that time I did go to see Mr. Milosevic, and I felt that something was wrong, because for the first time after a long time I did not make up the delegation which would go to see the president. But nonetheless, I did take all the people that I considered were important, and they did attend the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And what was requested of you on that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was requested, as Mr. Milosevic put it - and Goran Hadzic said this too - that I should no -- that I was no longer necessary and that he had quite a few comments and criticisms, nor was I desirable, and that I had to be replaced. And I said, "All right, go ahead and replace me." But they couldn't replace me, and that is why they proposed a meeting, for this to be done in Belgrade. I did not agree to that; however, at Mr. Milosevic's proposal we withdrew the next day in the morning at 10.00 from our posts; Kojic Ilija, Slavko Dokmanovic, and myself, we withdrew.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You said that they could not replace you. Why could they not replace you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't actually say why. Had they been able to do so, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. they would have done that. Well, probably they didn't have the necessary power and authority. They needed support from Mr. Milosevic, and they got that support.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In relation to this criticism against you, was there a -- the disconnection of a pipeline between Djeletovci and Pancevo involved?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. We're not getting the interpretation again. Could you try again, please, Mr. Milanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right. That was one of the criticisms made against me, but it was not the right one, that I had done it on my own arbitrarily, turned off the Djeletovci-Pancevo pipeline. I did this in collaboration -- in agreement with Milutinovic, who at that time was the foreign minister, and Tomic, who was at the time the director of the oil company in Serbia. As the embargo had been lifted after Dayton, Serbia was able to import oil. And for it to be able to import oil, our pipeline had to be extinguished for the pipeline passing through Croatia to Pancevo to be able to be operational.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You have described in your statement the -- your frequent disputes with Milan Martic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And in relation to that, I would like to refer to tab 28 of the Exhibit binder 549 as an example to this dispute with Milan Martic, and we do not need to go further into this.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Just this one question: Did Mr. Milosevic call you in regard of disputes with Milan Martic in relation to the officer Sladojevic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Mr. Milosevic called me, probably not personally, but his secretary did, and the topic of discussion was the commander of the 11th Corps. That was the corps of Srem and Baranja, the Srem-Baranja Corps. And Milan Martic wanted to change -- replace Sladojevic. He had wanted to do so several months prior to that. At a meeting, this was agreed although I did not accept this decision and Sladojevic's replacement did not take place. The next time, several months later, he probably complained to Mr. Milosevic and said that he would like to make some personnel changes in the 11th Corps but that he couldn't do so because I was in the way. So I was called up, and Mr. Milosevic told me that Martic -- that this was something that Martic wanted to do but that he was having problems with me and that I should give in, which I did, and the replacement took place after a brief period of time. And instead of General Sladojevic, we had General Loncar.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you in June 1995 intercept a transport of 8 million dinars from the SDK Ilok to Knin? And if so, did Mr. Milosevic get involved in this?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this did happen. One evening I was called up by Slavko Dokmanovic and the director of the SDK in Vukovar, and this was around 12.00 in the evening, that the operation was underway of withdrawing money from the SDK in Ilok and to have it illegally transferred to Knin, without any lawful or legal decision of the Krajina region, of the Krajina bank. I checked this out. I believed Dokmanovic and the director of the SDK of Vukovar when they said that it was illegal, and I reported it to the police, and the police stopped the kombi at the border carrying 8 million dinars, and these funds were returned to the area. Mr. Milosevic had no part in this at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did he call you on this occasion and inquire?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After a certain period of time, Martic requested the money, and he complained with the president, and this was a topic discussed at a meeting. However, we didn't enter into the details of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: During the preparation of your testimony, did you listen to a variety of intercepted conversation?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And did you sign a declaration related to the voices that you recognised?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's the special exhibit binder 551, and the first tab is actually this declaration that the witness made.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you know these people that you recognised from personal conversations and also from their public appearances?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostly from personal contacts, but a fewer number from the media.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really think it's absurd for such a witness to confirm intercepted conversations. Most of these conversations are between Radovan Karadzic and Jovica Stanisic. They're not even very important. But that is not the point. What is the point is that he cannot be considered qualified to say whether those conversations are authentic or not. He had nothing to do with Karadzic. He may have met Stanisic three times in his life.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's all a matter of evidence, and the witness can go -- give evidence about the knowledge which he has or doesn't have about these speakers. No doubt the Prosecution are going to cover that. And if --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did -- how familiar were you with the voice of Stanisic, as an example?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within a range of 1 to 5, I would say 4. I would give it 4, a mark of 4.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you know him from personal -- did you know his voice from personal contacts you had?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And in relation to Kertes?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same would apply to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We have already addressed some of these people, but what about Legija? How did -- how were you -- how familiar were you with his voice?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know his voice well.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: From personal contacts?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And the person Simatovic, that you identified, how do you know his voice?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know him personally too.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And in relation to Karadzic, how would you know his voice?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met him only once, in 1991, but I know that voice from the media.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And in relation to Sokolovic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met him several times too.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And Simatovic, Franko Simatovic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We've already said that I met him several times.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And lastly, Mladic, General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never met him, but he has a specific voice recognisable through the media.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In relation to these intercepts, I just want to ask you in relation to tab 10 of that binder. There is an intercepted conversation between Mr. Milosevic and Mr. Karadzic referring to the persons Ratko and Vladan. Who would that be? Can you help us with that? It's a very short -- yes, please. If you recall who that is. It's tab 10, and it's a very brief intercept. And just the reference to Ratko and Vladan.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that conversation because it wasn't long ago. And I assume from the conversation that they were referring to certain specialised legal matters and that references were made to Ratko. And what was the other name? I forgot.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Vladan. Vladan.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And Vladan. Ratko Markovic would be the vice-premier, and Kutlesic, who was also a counsellor -- I can't remember his exact position. But I know Mr. Ratko Markovic in person, and I know that he worked in the government as the vice-president of the government or Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. vice-premier.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you're speaking of the government of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And in two of the conversations where we have Arkan and Legija, there is a code number used as number 99. Do you know what code number 99 refers to?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Arkan's code during the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And in tab 23 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, if you could tell me where we can find Vladan and Ratko.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: That's in tab 10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I couldn't find it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, you have to actually look into the B/C/S version, because the correct -- the correct spelling is in the B/C/S version. And in the English version there is a -- a mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Was it translated as "Laden" and "Ratio"?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, and when you see the original, it's Vladan and Ratko. So there is a wrong translation to that effect. I'm sorry, I forgot to mention that. And the two intercepts that I just mentioned with the code number, that's tab 21 and tab 23.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And in relation to tab 23, on the -- actually, at the end of this conversation, there is reference made to a -- a person Bojovic. Do you know to which -- do you know this person Bojovic and to which formation he belongs? It's a conversation between -- it's tab 23, a conversation between Legija and the headquarters of the Serb Volunteer Guard. It's actually the last -- the last line before the greetings.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that conversation because Legija was speaking to an unknown person. I assume it was the secretary of Mr. Raznjatovic. And she says, "Say hello to Bojovic," so I assume this applies to a soldier who was in the field together with Legija.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But you are not familiar with a soldier Bojovic among the Arkan's?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in a haze I could sort of recollect, but I can't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Just a very few -- a final question in relation to the Skorpions. You have described the Skorpions being involved and sent to the Bihac region. When they were in this region, to whom were they subordinated then?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were subordinated to the command of the army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And to get to the battlefield in Bihac, would they have to cross through Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were the Serbian authorities aware of that movement?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But we thought at the time that we -- there were -- that no one was violating any agreement, as that was one army.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What do you mean "one army"?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm referring to the army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. The region of Srem and Baranja was physically separated from the lower part of Krajina and there no was no other way of reaching the lower part of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you also mentioned the Skorpions being present in Trnovo in Bosnia in 1994. How did the Skorpions get there? Would they have to go through Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Again, the Republika Srpska was physically separated and there was no way of reaching it except through the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And while the Skorpions were in Trnovo, to whom were they subordinated?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the MUP of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You described the deployment of the Skorpions in Kosovo, and especially the first deployment when you accompanied them a short way. At that time, was there a mobilisation in Serbia underway?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The Skorpions went to Kosovo seven or eight days after the NATO bombing. And on the first day of the bombing, in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, a state of war was proclaimed, which meant that the mobilisation was proclaimed and ongoing.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And why did Medic call you instead of just getting mobilised with the JNA -- or the VJ, in this case?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Medic called me because he didn't want him and his men, the men he knew from Slavonia, to go under the command of the army of Yugoslavia. He wanted to go as part of the MUP of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And finally, Ovcara. You have described how you heard and got aware of the Ovcara mass grave and how you informed Colonel Grahovac about this fact. In relation to this event, we have tab 32 of the Exhibit 549. And it's a report, actually, from Colonel Grahovac in relation to his findings. It's the last -- it's the last tab in the binder that you have. And in the last paragraph, there is a reference saying, "According to our intelligence, bodies have allegedly been moved from Ovcara site." It's on the last page, the last paragraph. And -- it's the last paragraph, the bodies. Do you know who -- if bodies were removed and who did that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only on the basis of rumours. But this was never proven, and it is well known that in 1998 the bodies were found.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have a little bit -- or I have taken a little bit too much time. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just deal, if you would, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff -- let's just tidy this up. The exhibit binder for the intercepts 551, marked for identification so far, of course, like the other intercepts, tab 2 is the compact disk.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And at the moment the Registry don't seem to have it, we don't seem to have it. Obviously it -- that should be tidied up and we should give it --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. We have copies just made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: At the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, hand them in, if you would, at the break.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you have seen that I have skipped two documents because there was no time to deal with that, but they are not so crucial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I can see that. If the legal officer would come up, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I begin, Mr. May, could I at least know what's under tab 2 on this disk that no one has received, and now it is being tendered into evidence following the testimony of this witness? Could I at least be told what it is?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's the -- according to the document -- yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: As I understand it, it's the compact disk containing all the intercepts.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Exactly, Your Honour. The declaration is tab 1, the CD is tab 2, and tab 3 to 27 is -- are the transcripts. And on the CD there is actually in the order how they were played the -- the intercepted conversations are played.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Just for the record, so it is quite clear that not a single of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. those -- one of those conversations was played here in the presence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, would you deal with the point that the accused is making. He doesn't seem to have understood the position. Were these intercepts played to the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, they were all played to the witness in the order of the declaration and also in the order of the CD. It's -- it would just take too much time to have it all produced here in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're not -- we're not having them played here, for that reason. But he signed a declaration that he's identified the voices.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Your Honour, he did that. And it is indicated exactly which voice he recognised and which not. And he does not make any comments further than that in the declaration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Milanovic, tell me, to the best of your recollection, when did tensions start in Eastern Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tensions in Eastern Slavonia started in May 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was there any tension during the time of the elections, prior to the elections in 1990?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was some tension in 1990 and in 1991 in the area of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what was happening in 1990?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is well known that the elections were being prepared in the Republic of Croatia. It is also common knowledge that the HDZ party came into power, headed by Tudjman. It is also well known that from the constitution the Serbs were thrown out as a nation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When were they eliminated from the constitution?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly, but I think it was several months after the HDZ came to power.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, when the constitution was changed and a number of laws promulgated - I assume you remember that - what was the effect this had among the Serb population? I'm not talking about the whole of Croatia, I'm just talking about the area that you are familiar with, that is, the area of Eastern Slavonia. So on the basis of your own knowledge, not on the basis of the newspapers or political debates that were going on.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The effect among people was fear as to what would happen next.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Would you please describe that fear for me, what kind of fear it was.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: People feared because the Serbs had still not forgotten 1941 and they felt that problems could occur on an ethnic basis, that they might lose their rights, such as the right to employment and the other rights they enjoyed, and people were afraid and they started to organise themselves into their own national parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, to the best of your recollection, when did the first cases of Serbs being fired from public services occur? For example, the police and other public services.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regarding public services, I can't know everything but I can remember with respect to the police. I think these happenings occurred in January, February, March 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were the Serbs expelled from the police en masse?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say that they were dismissed en masse, but they were fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So from the beginning of 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me, when were the first acts of violence against Serbs in Eastern Slavonia? Not counting these expulsions from work but physical violence, physical attacks.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A major incident occurred on the 2nd of May in Borovo Selo, when the Croatian police came and there was an armed conflict at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And before Borovo Selo, were there individual incidents, murders, cases of people disappearing that you're aware of?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When was that in Borovo Selo?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 2nd of May, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were you in Borovo Selo at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And how far is Borovo Selo from your place? What did you learn about that? What had happened in Borovo Selo in 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my place is about 20 kilometres away from Borovo Selo, and I learnt that the Croatian police left from Osijek and Vinkovci, that they went in two buses - or several buses, I can't remember exactly - and that they started out to take down the Serb flag, which had been flying in the centre of Borovo Selo on the local community building.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what happened then?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was an armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the elections in 1990. You took part in those elections; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that in Eastern Slavonia the largest number of the Serb electorate voted for the League of Communists of Croatia, the SPD party, because there were deputies on that -- those parties' lists that were elected to the Sabor, or Croatian parliament, from that region? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At those elections in Slavonia, the Serbian Democratic Party had not been set up yet; that is to say, the party for which the Serbs voted in the other parts of Croatia where it had been established. And so for the most part the Serbs voted for Racan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, did the citizens of Serb ethnicity vote for the League of Communists of Croatia, the SDP, believing that the party was in favour of Yugoslavia and that it was against the war, that it was in favour of peace, in fact?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That party declared itself in that way at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And how -- now, I'm talking about you as a citizen. How did this affect you, your friends, your neighbours, the citizens of Eastern Slavonia? How did this change in the constitution affect you, that the Serbs had been expelled from the constitution, that the chequer-board emblem was introduced, and all the rest of it? How did that affect and influence you, for example?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we didn't feel at ease.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You didn't feel comfortable? Is that it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you remember when in Croatia the volunteer detachments began to be formed or, rather, the different paramilitary formations which were nationalistic and very hostile towards the Serb population? Since when do you know of their existence, for example?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, roughly from the middle of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that already in the summer of 1990 that mass provocations started, pressure exerted on the JNA and its members, their family members, and so on and so forth? Would that be true?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I knew at the time, there were individual cases of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you remember that in the course of 1990 over 70 cases of provocation and physical attacks were registered against members of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember that piece of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, then. So you just remember the individual attacks; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Very well. Fine. Now, tell me this, please: Before the active conflicts, such as the one that started in Borovo Selo, et Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. cetera, do you recall that the members of MUP stormed the police stations in which there were mostly Serbs and later on in the evening hours they confiscated weapons which existed there for the reserve police force, new police stations were opened up, mostly where the Serbs lived or in a mixed environment, with a mixed population? Do you remember those events?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember those events, and they went parallel to this situation: The Yugoslav People's Army confiscated weapons from the Territorial Defence on the one side and the MUP of Croatia confiscated weapons from its reserve force, which was predominantly populated by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What you want to say is in the areas where there was a Serb population; is that where the weapons were taken away from the reserve police force? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, roughly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, is it also true that following orders from the Presidency of the SFRY, which were common knowledge that, the Serbs in Croatia, especially in the Knin Krajina, they returned their weapons; whereas, the Croatian forces did not do so?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you remember that at the time certain mobilisation had taken place into formations that were established, the Croatian National Guards Corps, for example, and the reserve composition of the MUP of Croatia? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I remember is that the MUP of the Republic of Croatia reinforced its reserve composition in the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And have you heard of the National Guards Corps, the ZNG?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later on, when there was active operation, when that started I heard about it. But I don't know when this was actually established.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, tell me this: Is it true that the arming of the Serbs became intensified only after the SFRY Presidency meeting held on the 12th of March, 1991, when the proposal was rejected from the Secretary of National Defence to introduce a state of emergency in the country and when the attempt fell through made by the Presidency in December 1990 to disarm the paramilitaries in the SFRY?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is my position that the Serbs started arming themselves when they saw that there was -- that they couldn't count on political negotiations and that the possibility of war breaking out was there. I think that that's when this parallel armament took place, that is to say, the Serbs began arming themselves and so did the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And do you know when this illegal import of weapons or purchase of weapons for the Croatian paramilitaries began? Did you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did hear about it, but I can't say for sure what the date was when this started, but I do know that Croatia imported arms through Hungary and our army let that happen. And I also know that there was a plane of some kind which landed at the airport and then this -- these weapons were confiscated. I think that it landed at Zagreb airport, and then it was forced to be taken and go on to Belgrade. I remember those two details.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, do you remember when the campaign started, launched by the Croatian authorities, with respect to the blockade of military JNA facilities on the territory of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that there was a blockade. Now, when it took place exactly, I can't remember. But I assume at the same time that you asked a question before this, as the political negotiations fell through, the situation became more complicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, in your view, would you say that the population - and we're talking about the Serb population - was exposed realistically to a danger of its life? Was this a realistic threat, faced with a situation of that kind, in the general mood that prevailed at the time, after the enactment of the constitution, after they had been dismissed from their work, after all the pressure, and finally after the physical conflicts, was this fear justified?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The fear was justified, both on the Serb side and on the Croatian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, tell me, please: What caused fear in the Serb population of Eastern Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was fear in Eastern Slavonia due to the events that came to pass in Borovo Selo on the 2nd of May, for example. That caused quite a lot of fear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And is it true that the JNA from the very beginning, that is to say, from those first conflicts, endeavoured to separate the conflicting parties or, rather, to calm the situation down?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the very beginning, yes. However, as the political negotiations showed that there was no hope for success, so the Croats started leaving the army and the army was replenished with Serbs from the regular formations or from the reservists, so that the army in fact became Serb more and more and on the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And is it true that it was precisely due to the efforts made by the JNA to prevent conflicts and to stand between the two sides that in the field, on the ground where you were, that your various local volunteer detachments had a very negative relationship towards the army and criticised it and said that they were traitors precisely because the army wanted to be neutral and to separate the two conflicting parties? I'm sure you remember those events.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were cases of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At that time, the JNA was deployed throughout the territory of Yugoslavia; isn't that right, Mr. Milanovic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we're talking about the period up to the 2nd of May, 1991, then the answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, wasn't it there throughout 1991 as well?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure actually when the events in Slovenia took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. We're not talking about Slovenia now, we're talking about Croatia. There's somebody else who's going to talk about Slovenia. Tell me now, please: You were later the deputy or assistant defence minister, isn't that right, so you delved in politics in a way, right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Isn't it true that in that year of 1990 and 1991 that the army did not meddle in politics at all and it exclusively dealt with its own affairs and assignments, the protection of its units and efforts to separate the two conflicting parties to prevent an all-out conflict from breaking out?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for 1990, I don't know, I can't say. But as to the end of 1991 or, rather, the middle of 1991, that would be true, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, is it true that the relationship of the local Serb population at that time towards the JNA was such that they were ready even to enter into a conflict with members of the JNA to prevent military equipment and armament being taken away from the territory of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that in Eastern Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, there were no such instances.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it true that by the end of -- until the end of 1991 the army was considered to be the army of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, that it wasn't a Serb army, and that its cadres and staff were not made up of only Serb members? I assume you know that.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was mixed -- was it mixed?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that in April 1992, in the JNA there were still about 600 soldiers who were Croats; although in January 1992, for example, Croatia had already been recognised internationally, by the international community, the famous premature recognition of Croatia came about. Do you remember that piece of information, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that, but I do know that there were Croats still in the army. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you remember this piece of information relating to the air force; that more than half the fliers were not Serbs or Montenegrins, that they were members of other ethnic groups, in fact?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have that piece of information available.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And when the conflict started in Croatia, under the circumstances that you are testifying about, was this situation, generally speaking, in that area a situation of some kind of a civil war?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how I would call it, but the war broke out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But I'm asking you, was it a civil war? And let me clarify my question: Did anyone commit aggression?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's just answered the question. He doesn't know. And characterising the war, what type of war, will be a matter for the Trial Chamber. It's not a matter for the witness. Now, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, these are historical facts. You can decide whatever you will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, it's not a historical fact. It's the type of war it was. It's a matter of interpretation and may even be a matter of law, which we'll have to decide. It's not for the witness to say. You can ask him if he saw any Serbs attack Croatia or something of the sort if you wish, if that's your point you want to make. But you can't ask him about characterising matters -- what may be matters of law.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I asked him whether he saw Croatian paramilitary units attacking Serbs, and he said he did, he had seen them. Serb settlements, and he said yes. Now, if you want me to ask him what you want ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you, Mr. Milanovic, did the Serbs commit aggression against Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stand by my earlier answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You can't give me a direct answer? Do you believe that there is any possibility of saying that the Serbs committed aggression against Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have answered the question put to me. Now, this is already politics.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Tell me, is it true that refugees from your areas in particular - and one might say from the whole of Croatia - started moving out in large waves already in October 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, even before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What were those refugees fleeing from? Mostly to Serbia; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostly to Serbia; yes, they fled there. And at the beginning of August, active combat operations started in the area and the Yugoslav People's Army joined in, as well as the Serbs, and on the other side were the Croats. Then there were large numbers of refugees on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Milanovic. In paragraph 3, you say that your family fled to Serbia; isn't that right, as refugees?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So this happened as early as May 1991, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How many such families started fleeing already in May 1991? Surely it wasn't just your family.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In your previous question, you said October 1991, and I answered earlier than that. And after the events of the 2nd of May, quite a large number of women and children went to Serbia. And then they would come back and go away again, and so on, but most of them left in August 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it true that through the JNA you endeavoured to reach a non-aggression agreement with the Croatian side?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Everything that I have said in my statement is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I am unable, like the other side, to ask you whether what is written in your statement is correct. I have to put questions to you. So you endeavoured through the JNA to reach a non-attack agreement with Croatia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But in spite of that, these members of the National Guards Corps, of which you don't know when it was formed, attacked you. And in paragraph 3, you mention this. You say, "The National Guards Corps attacked us. We were attacked by the ZNG," et cetera. So in spite of your endeavours to come to an agreement that you wouldn't attack one another, you were attacked nevertheless?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And your village is called Palaca; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Explain to me, please, since you say that a TV crew from ZDF from Germany was filming the consequences of the attack on Palaca from Laslovo, and they showed this on television as if it was the opposite situation, as if you from Palaca had attacked Laslovo; is that right, Mr. Milanovic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So they fraudulently presented that the Serbs had attacked the Croatian side; whereas, the reality was the opposite. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I've already answered that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Don't say to me, "I've already answered that question." Just tell me, was that a falsification?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Just a moment, Mr. Milosevic. We waste time. And your comment to the witness was unfair. He had answered the question. He'd said what he could see. Now, whether any inference is to be drawn from that is not a matter for the witness. So again, it's an example of you trying to argue with him all the time and then rebuking him wrongly for not answering the question. He was quite right. You could put -- make your points and then move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's move on. I just wanted to establish what the witness has said, that the representation was the opposite, that the Serbian side had attacked the Croats instead of the other way around.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We can understand the point. You don't need to repeat it all the time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not repeating it all the time, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that in May 1991, Mr. Milanovic, in the area in which you were there were Croatian troops and your village were shelled daily by about 600 projectiles? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. It started around the 26th of June and onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So in view of such a situation, is it true that the Serbs were fleeing from the area because of the pressure and the war operations engaged in by the forces of the opposite side?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be quite precise in giving my answer to this question, Palaca was on the very separation line between the Serbs and the Croats, and it was the first place on the route from Zagreb-Osijek to Vukovar. And fighting had started around Vukovar at that time, and as the fighting for Vukovar started in which the Yugoslav People's Army took an active part, so the attacks increased by the Croatian side against the first defence lines towards the west.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Wait a moment, please. So this -- this village of yours was mostly Serb, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, mostly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the next village towards the west is Laslovo, which has a majority Croatian population?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Hungarian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see, Hungarian. So tell me, how was this confrontation line established? Those settlements have been there for hundreds of years or decades, at least; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether this was any coincidence, but roughly since the events in Borovo Selo, a battalion of the Yugoslav People's Army Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. pulled out of Osijek and came to Palaca and stayed there until April 1992, and that is how, in my judgement, the line was formed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We must now adjourn. It's time for the break. We'll adjourn now for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milanovic, do you remember the end of October, or to be more precise, the 31st of October, 1991, when 15 villages were cleansed of the municipality of Grubisno Polje, 15 Serb villages?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember that event. Only I have not remembered the exact date, but that is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you remember the 13th of December, when more than 100 settlements in the municipalities of Slatina, Daruvar, Slavonska Pozega, were also cleansed? This is something that you should be aware of.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware of those events in Western Slavonia, but I wasn't there, and I heard about them and I don't know the exact number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And are you familiar with data on destroyed Serbian churches or the events around Pakrac, Pakracka Poljana, the mass execution of Serbs in Marino Selo and Pakracka Poljana? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the media, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What were you at the time when this was happening? What was the position that you held?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If this was before the 19th of December, then I was assistant minister for transport. If it was after the 19th of December, 1991, I was Assistant for Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you were only informed from the media even though you were an assistant minister?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, did you hear of the Operation Flash and how many Serbs were killed on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard of the Operation Flash, and I do know that Serbs were killed, but I don't know exactly how many.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did you hear of the killing of women and children on that occasion as well?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did hear about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And tell me, do you have any knowledge of the number of people - and I mean Serbs - how many thousands of them were deported from those areas on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They say between 150.000 and 200.000. Now, what the exact figure is, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any direct knowledge as to the number of camps for Serbs in Croatia during the war?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know that there were camps, but I don't know how many.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any idea how many Serbs were held in those camps?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have any idea, but I do know that there were Serbs held there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Since you mentioned Plitvice in paragraph 5 of your statement, what happened at Plitvice and when?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can recollect, this was in August 1990, when a Serb delegation was going to a meeting. Whether it was in Knin or Lika, I don't know exactly. And they were arrested there, a couple of Serbs, headed by Goran Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And those Serbs who were arrested on that occasion, had they committed any kind of violence or anything like that due to which they needed to be arrested?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, they did not commit any act of violence which would warrant their arrest.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And why were they arrested, then?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only assume that Croatia knew that Goran Hadzic and this group that was arrested were politically active in the area of Slavonia and Krajina, and that is why they arrested them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were they members of the Serbian Democratic Party at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they were at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was the Serbian Democratic Party registered in a regular fashion with the Croatian authorities as a political party?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it wasn't registered in the territory -- territory of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, but I am sure that it was registered in Knin. And it was acting as a party, and it participated in the multi-party elections in Knin, Donji Lapac, and other places. Yes, in those places but not in Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Plitvice was in the area where it was registered; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Ask do you remember raids on the 2nd of March, 1991, when 600 members of the special MUP forces raided Serb houses, searched them, and mistreated their inhabitants?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This did not happen in Slavonia. I don't know whether it occurred in the lower part of Krajina. I'm not familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you do not know about any event that did not take place in your area; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of them, yes, as of the 19th of December, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that in the environs of Pokrovac [as interpreted] the Croatian forces opened fire on military columns without any reason, when even the city hospital was hit? Do you remember those events? This was in Pakrac.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that particular event, but I know that JNA columns were attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, when that conflict occurred in Plitvice, between members of the National Guards Corps and the local Serbs, was the role of the JNA merely to separate them?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether the JNA was involved in Plitvice in 1990. I'm not sure about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And tell me, the events in Plitvice, were they the cause for the formation of the Serbian National Council?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure, but that could be so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And when was the Serbian National Council formed? Was it after Plitvice?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the exact date. I wasn't a member of the Serbian National Council at the time. But it was roughly in that period of 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 5, you say, "After the events in Plitvice in August 1990 ..." and then you mention the names, the Serbian National Council was formed and Goran Hadzic was the president. You say for yourself that you were elected in September or somewhat earlier. I think it was at Milenko Zivkovic's suggestion.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the first part was in 1990, and the second part that you mentioned was in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since you mention events in Vukovar, tell me, please, is it true that before the JNA intervened, the barracks in Vukovar was blocked by the National Guards Corps and cut off so that soldiers and officers for 20 days went without electricity, water, and supplies?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true. With the beginning of the conflict in the territory of the town of Vukovar and its surroundings, the barracks found itself under siege.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it true that apart from being blocked for 20 days, it was also attacked with various shells and already on the 14th of September, 1991, among JNA members there were casualties, dead and wounded?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I know that there were conflicts. Now, the exact number of dead and wounded, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you do know that there were dead and wounded.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I say that I do know that there were dead and wounded, but I don't know how many.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was this already in September? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: August, end of August, September, sometime around then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you remember that General Kadijevic tasked Admiral Brovet, who was his deputy, to inform the European Troika and Lord Carrington about this, who was at the time the chairman of the Conference on Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember. And I think that Admiral Brovet did come to the area and engaged in negotiations between the JNA, the Serbs, and the Croats, with some other members of the Presidency of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And how much time elapsed after those incidents, that is, the blocking of the barracks, the casualties in the barracks; how much after that did the JNA intervene to deblock the barracks in relation to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, the JNA participated in lifting the blockade of the barracks and in liberating Vukovar from the end of August 1991 until the 18th of November, 1991, when the town of Vukovar actually fell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it true that in Vukovar there was no preconceived plan on the part of the Serbs and the JNA, that the JNA forces in Vukovar sought to deblock the barracks, that they were constantly fired at and the JNA soldiers only responded to that fire?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that was so at the beginning, but later on the decision was taken to attack the town of Vukovar itself and liberate it from the Croatian forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, as you've mentioned Ovcara, tell me what you knew about the events at Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, when Ovcara took place, I knew nothing about it. Several months later, however, upon the insistence of the international community and mostly at that time Mrs. Albright -- and she was the United States ambassador to the United Nations at the time, and she came to the area and asked around, whether there was anything there. So at that time, it was difficult to learn anything. And after talking to me sometime at the beginning of 1991, when she returned to the United Nations she asked that UN forces be sent there, and they were deployed and the forces were there until 1997 or 1998, when there was the digging up at Ovcara and the discovery of the bodies there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And is it true that you had no information about the events linked to Ovcara at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it already -- also correct that you tried to learn about those events and to do so you talked to a large number of people? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the answers you were given from the locals of Vukovar is that there was nothing there.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So at that time, you didn't know anything about that either, did you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, I knew nothing, because the town of Vukovar was cut off from the area I was in - let's call it the Erdut area - until Vukovar was liberated. And that took place during the liberation of Vukovar and it was skilfully concealed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, let's make a slight digression here. You were the main source of information that you gave to Radovan Stojicic, is that right, about the events in those parts?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And since you knew nothing about Ovcara, I assume that Radovan Stojicic could not have known anything either. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, while he was in the region, I don't think he knew anything about Ovcara, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Now, you, in fact, when Albright asked you to have the UN forces sent there in order to secure the area, you told her that you had nothing against that. You gave your permission, and then the UN soldiers took up their positions in the locality. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.
