utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the political position taken by the leadership was to allow the UN to control the area, including the Ovcara area.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the Vance Owen Plan, yes, that would be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it also true that according to what you knew about Ovcara, that the JNA or the MUP of Serbia had nothing to do with it, or anybody else under the command or control of the JNA or MUP of Serbia or generally the leadership in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that Radovan Stojicic had nothing to do with it. I didn't say the JNA. The JNA in that particular area was stationed there. There was an army brigade there and the entire region or area, if we call it Srem, that is, the south of Vukovar, was under the control of the Yugoslav People's Army. And that was its area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever learn that any of the members of the JNA were at Ovcara when all this happened?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't even know to this day what actually happened at Ovcara, who committed what took place there, and especially then. I had no idea then at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, what can you tell us about Lovas? According to what you learnt, as far as I am able to conclude, the JNA had nothing to do -- or any individual could have been under the control of the JNA or linked to Serbia at all in any way with respect to anybody from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the same is true for Lovas as is true for Ovcara. A state of war had been proclaimed, war law was prevalent, and all the civilians and everybody bearing arms, whether the TO or the reservists or whoever, volunteers, they were under the command of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you set up your own Territorial Defence at the time, did you not, in Eastern Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, in fact?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did. But it was always subordinated to the Yugoslav People's Army and acted under the command of the JNA, from August until the end of the war operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what do you consider to be the end of the war operations?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my mind, the end of the war operations was the end of November 1991, in the area of Slavonia. Now, of course, there were certain places where active operations ended earlier on and others where it went on later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Milanovic. Can we take it that you're not challenging the fact that after November 1991 there were no operations in the area? Right up until the signing of the Erdut agreement. So to all intents and purposes, there was no war in the area.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There wasn't a war, but there was sporadic -- there were sporadic operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What kind of sporadic operations?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for example, the Croatian army would sometimes fire a shell at our side, and we would retaliate. So sporadic gunfire. It will never be quite clear who did what first, but it was between the two sides. And then, for example, there was some small mortar attacks on the Miljevac plateau, the Maslenicki bridge, Western Slavonia, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. That isn't your particular area, and we'll come to that later on. But can we take it, can we note that once the areas under UN protection were established and the UN protection zone was in fact established, which covered Eastern Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, once the UNPAs were set up, there were no attacks from the Serb side on any territory outside the zone, nor were there any attacks within the zone either?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think we understood each other with respect to the previous question. When these events were taking place, then there was some mortar fire and mortar shelling, but to a small extent, nothing intense that -- to follow on to your previous question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, once the JNA, pursuant to the agreement, had left the territory of Croatia, the Serb side or, rather, the Serb army of Krajina or the Territorial Defence or the police force, did they ever launch any kind of attack on territory under Croatian control? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never. It never launched any kind of attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Judging by what you say in your statement, from Palaca, those of you who were in Palaca had been given 50 rifles from Bobota, ammunition as well, but you don't know how those weapons came to be in Bobota, do you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, no, how it came to be in Bobota.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And when was the new Territorial Defence formed of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem? When was that formed?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The new Territorial Defence of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem was formed between the 2nd of May and August. It was first of all active in different areas and wasn't linked up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So it was established after the events in Borovo Selo in the local communities, which means in the villages in actual fact; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, villages and Beli Manastir, those places.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And as I can see from your statement, of the old structures, the Territorial Defence was just taken over from the old organisation in Beli Manastir. But that was placed under the Territorial Defence of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem as well; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. All right. Now, as the Territorial Defence in Croatia was a national selective body, is it true that that was the reason for which the Serbs organised themselves on the principle of the local staffs and commands in the area, defence?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what the word means.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But in the Territorial Defence of that area, there were other ethnic groups too, not only Serbs, who also wished to defend the area.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, especially in Baranja.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At that time, this Territorial Defence was not under JNA control, the one that was established in the villages and the other localities more or less spontaneously; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said up until August it was not, but after August it did come under the command of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, is it true that that Territorial Defence, once it had been established, was in fact a form of popular protection? And according to my sources of information, it was not even on good terms with the JNA. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At all events, it was established as a form of protection or defence. "Territorial Defence" is the term used, and it means what it says. Now -- well, it was on good terms with the JNA. The JNA did not launch any operations in the area without the TO taking part, or vice versa, that the TO went into any action which was not under the command of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what about the various formations that certain parties set up themselves? What about those?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All those formations set up by the parties - and I mean parties from the Republic of Serbia, the Radicals, I think, the Radical Party - were under the command of the TO and the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you mean to say that the party formations became included into the JNA structure generally speaking?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whoever bore arms or wore a uniform on the territory of Slavonia, Baranja, and Srem was under the command of the JNA, and for several months you couldn't move from one place to another unless you received permission from the JNA to move around the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, was that done in a general effort to avoid conflict, or was the intention otherwise?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was done pursuant to orders because there was a war on and the danger of war, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The danger of war. But we have just observed and noted that after November 1991 there was -- there were no war operations in the area. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm saying -- I'm talking about the period from August to the end of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You were appointed traffic and communications minister at the proposal of Milenko Zivkovic. Couldn't you tell us who Milenko Zivkovic is?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milenko Zivkovic was at the time a member of the National Serb Council, and he was born in the area, and I think that he was the only one that I did know out of all the names I listed. Before the war, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And the Defence Ministry, at the proposal of Radlovic Predrag; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So in both instances it was organised internally in Eastern Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. Your appointment and nomination, nobody influenced that from Serbia, did they?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me now, please: You say that on the 28th of November, 1991, you say that in paragraph 10, in actual fact - and you have the statement before you, I believe, your notes - you say that in Erdut, on the 28th of November, 1991, all the operations had been completed. Isn't that right? There were no war conflicts after that.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not 100 per cent certain whether it was actually the 28th of November or perhaps the 10th of December, but anyway, I'm 99 per cent correct that it was the 28th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But that was a time when there were no more war conflicts going on; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then you say that in addition to the ministers in the government of SAO Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, the meeting was attended by Radovan Stojicic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me this, please: As you mention the presence of Radovan Stojicic, who else, to the best of your recollections, from the MUP of Serbia attended the meeting with him? Somebody who worked in the Ministry of the Interior of Serbia, for example?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When Radovan Stojicic, Badza, came to the Slavonia area and became commander of the Territorial Defence, with him came -- well, I can't remember exactly, but about some 15 members of his unit. They came with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And do you know that Radovan Stojicic, as a patriot and volunteer, came there to help you? He didn't come there with any unit of the MUP of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Radovan Stojicic, Badza, came to the area as a patriot, but I'm not sure that he came as a volunteer or perhaps following somebody's instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Wouldn't it be logical, if he came in any other capacity, for him to have a unit with him? In your statement, you mentioned --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can't ask him that. You can't ask him what's logical. What you can ask the witness is whether when Badza came he came with a unit or did he come by himself. Could you help us with that, Mr. Milanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When Radovan Stojicic, Badza, came on the 21st, I think it was, September, I heard the story that he had come because the army was not managing to free Vukovar and that he wanted to assist in the control and command of the Territorial Defence and its cooperation with the Yugoslav People's Army, and he came with some 15 men and his unit. I think the unit at the time did not -- I mean, in Belgrade, the SAJ, didn't number more than 20 or 25 men on the outside.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And who did you hear that from that, he had come with 15 men in order to free Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I saw him come with my own eyes, and at a meeting of the government of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem it was stated that a man would come from the MUP of Serbia to be the commander of the TO and to link up all the forces in the area to liberate Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And tell me, who did you personally see, apart from what you heard, that he had come with some 15 men? Did you see those 15 men?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did see all 15 or so of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you claiming that those 15 men constituted a unit of some sort?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the story about a special anti-terrorist unit which numbered in Serbia 20 to 25 men, and if he comes with 15, then for me that is a unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let us leave that aside for the moment, what is a unit for you. I don't know how many men that unit numbered, but the fact that Badza had come as a volunteer to Slavonia, on what grounds do you believe that he came --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Just a moment. You're putting that he's a volunteer. The witness isn't accepting that he was a volunteer. Do you know -- do you know if he was a volunteer or not? I think you've already dealt with that, haven't you, Mr. Milanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll try once again to explain this. Radovan Stojicic, Badza, as I said, the reason for his coming was to liberate Vukovar. I mentioned the number of men. And this is rather a large number for a special unit. And he came with weapons and equipment and not for a moment was it my understanding that they were there on a voluntary basis, especially in view of several examples, as you requested. For example, the equipment and weapons and uniforms, the system of communications, their salaries, they received them in Serbia, and upon the completion of the assignment all of them, or at least the commanding staff, were promoted. For example, Badza came as a commander of a special unit of the MUP of Serbia, and while he was still with me, just prior to his return, he was appointed assistant minister of internal affairs. So it's not logical for somebody to volunteer to a combat area and then to be promoted. So this is one example. I could think of others.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please be kind enough and explain to me what was the role of Radovan Stojicic in those operations. Do you have information that Radovan Stojicic or any of his associates committed any kind of crime over there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That unit from the MUP of Serbia that was in the area never committed any crimes; of that, I am certain. But its role was significant. I remember exactly when they arrived on the 21st of September, and the halting of an operation on Vukovar for some 15 days or a month until a system of control and command was established, together with General Bratic [phoen], and later when he was killed on the 4th of November, then with his successor they met on a daily basis and they drew up a plan and led the operation for the liberation of Vukovar, which started on the 4th of November and ended on the 18th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So that means within the framework of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my statement, I said that the JNA dominated the area until Badza arrived. After Badza's arrival, the JNA gained in significance, and it was treated as a real TO, so that in every operation it was subordinated to the JNA, especially as the TO didn't have weapons and no mortars, cannon, or heavy weapons or self-propelled launchers or any other equipment. This was all in the possession of the JNA. And when Badza arrived, the TO gained in significance, and all operations were coordinated by the Yugoslav People's Army and the TO implemented them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it true that it was only in October 1991 that you considered yourself to be under the MUP and that was when Badza came there and you considered this to be a link with the MUP of Serbia? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite so. That is what was stated at a meeting of the government of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, that a man was coming from the MUP of Serbia who would take over the command of the TO and as soon as he arrived Goran Hadzic appointed him commander of the TO, a couple of days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So Goran Hadzic appointed him.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So no one from Serbia appointed him, did they?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think someone sent him from Serbia and Goran Hadzic just confirmed this in paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So this appointment carried out by Goran Hadzic, who was then what? The president of the area, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the Prime Minister of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Isn't that proof that Badza, who had come as a volunteer and places himself at the disposal --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. You must not put questions in that way. You've heard quite well what the witness has said about his being a volunteer. There's no point putting questions in a tendentious way which misrepresents what the witness has said. Now, move on to the next question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We have established that he was appointed by a decision of the Prime Minister of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, that is, Goran Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've been through this. Let's move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that there were several members of the MUP of Serbia who temporarily suspended their positions in the MUP of Serbia and went as volunteers to assist you in defending yourself? Are you aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were men from the MUP of Serbia, but I'm not familiar with their status regarding their employment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of a similar situation in the JNA, that is, that officers born in Bosnia, Croatia could go, and always voluntarily, to assist the army of Republika Srpska or the army of the Serbian Krajina, that is, to join the ranks of the fighters there? Because these were areas in which they were born, to which they belonged, and which they felt needed to be defended. So a similar situation existed with respect to many JNA members who then became members of the army of Republika Srpska of the Serbian army of Krajina; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were cases of people going voluntarily, but there were also cases of people going upon orders of the General Staff of the army of Yugoslavia to those areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know, as deputy defence minister, that such an order could only apply with respect to their emolument, social and material status, but not with respect to questions of control and command?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure what your question was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let me rephrase the question. Is it true that the army of Yugoslavia, or as you put it, the General Staff of the army of Yugoslavia, did it have command over the army of the Republic of Srpska Krajina or the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give a precise answer to that question, but I do know that the Serbian army of Krajina was dependent upon the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mean it received aid from them?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Depended on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And who was your commander? You were assistant defence minister. Was there a Main Staff of the Serbian army of Krajina? Was there a Supreme Commander who was also the president of the Republic of Serbian Krajina? Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was the Main Staff of the army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, and it was in command in the area of Krajina; sometimes not even there. But it was in command in the area, but I think that the commanders of the Serbian army of Krajina depended on the General Staff of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In the chain of command, did the general staff of the JNA command any operations in the territory of the Republic of Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So let's finish with that. Tell me, please, with respect to the structure of all those members of the Serbian army of Krajina, including civilians who took up arms to defend their homes and who formed the Serbian army of Krajina, where were those people from?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With respect to the territory of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, I can say that at the very beginning the TO was mostly composed of the local population. Then in a certain period of time some volunteers arrived who were either under the command of the TO or directly under the JNA, and the number was between 10 and 25 thousand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Of what?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: From Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the region of Srem and Baranja.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And how many out of those 25.000 soldiers of the Srem and Baranja region were volunteers from Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is difficult to say. You interrupted me. From August 1991 until November and December 1991, there were about 36.000 - about 36.000 - members of the army of Yugoslavia --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That is the JNA in 1991, not the VJ?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, the JNA. There were about 36.000 men. And it is hard to say how many volunteers there were, as there were volunteers both within the TO and within the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you about the Serbian army of Krajina, when that army was formed. In the area of Eastern Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, how many men did that army have when it -- the army was formed?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the TO or the Serbian army of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm very precise. I said the Serbian army of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serbian army of Krajina, I think, was officially formed for the first time in 1994, the Serbian army of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But in the meantime, it was called the TO of Krajina; is that right? Now, tell me, when the JNA withdrew from the territory of Croatia as a whole, that is, in 1992, what was the numerical strength of the TO in Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In April/May 1992, the JNA withdrew and the Vance Owen Plan came into effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us try and deal with this. Fist of all -- just a moment. So let us just clarify it. Before we -- before the Serb army of Krajina was formed, the accused has put that the body was called the TO of Krajina. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct. But it was acting in the following way: Up until the 26th of February, 1992, the TO operated in three areas; in the Knin area, in Western Slavonia, and Eastern Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. And when those three areas joined up, it was only then for the first time that the TO of the Republic of Serbian Krajina was established.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what was the numerical strength of that TO of the Republic of Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say exactly. But I can be precise with respect to Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, please do so, for that region.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were several stages. When the JNA withdrew, the Vance Owen Plan came into effect, and the double-key system. The TO was disbanded, and the Blue Brigades of the police guarded the border towards Croatia pursuant to the Vance Owen Plan. However, since the Croats violated the Vance Owen Plan, they attacked -- I can't remember whether it was the Miljevacka plateau or the Medak pocket, I can't remember exactly, but because of that the double-key system fell through, the TO was reactivated, and from then on it was the TO until 1994 and then the Serbian army of Krajina until Krajina fell. However, in the area of Slavonia, during the state of emergency, the state of war, the TO numbered some 20-odd thousand. And in a regular situation it numbered between 5 and 7 thousand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, we are talking about the emergency wartime situation, when the TO numbered some 20.000 men in Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, how many volunteers were there from Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult for me to be precise, but between 3 and 4 thousand, I think. I don't think I'd be wrong if I would put it at that figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Those who came to join the ranks of the Territorial Defence of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, tell me this, please: Once this Territorial Defence had been established, of Krajina, and the command structure put in place, was there a single defence minister or minister of the police or commander of the Main Staff of the Serb army of Krajina or Territorial Defence who was somebody born outside Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that all of them were born either -- or they originated, their roots were from Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And where do you get the piece of information, as you put it, that there were 3.000 volunteers from Serbia? Do you have any records of that, that there were so many, such a large number of volunteers? Because that would make it 10 per cent, 10 per cent of your forces made up of volunteers from Serbia. Where do you get that figure from? You must have had some records.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is based on a free -- a good but free assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But can you give me any reason on the basis of which you made that free assessment of yours? What were the grounds?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I do have reason to say that. As the ministry dealt with supplies for the army - this especially referred to uniforms, boots, that kind of thing, if I can put it that way - and then I know that those people would usually be given priority, because they were guests in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. If you dealt with their supplies and logistics, uniforms, et cetera, then you must have some document where this is evidenced, which records how much equipment you issued to those guests in the area, uniform, boots, et cetera, which would bear out what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we didn't keep records for us to say two or three units and then have special records for them, but they were deployed in the brigades and battalions. So we didn't have any separate records kept for that. That wasn't customary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So that means you don't have any records.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think anybody has any records of that kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before we go any further, Mr. Milosevic, there's just a matter I want to clarify. What dates are we talking about, Mr. Milanovic? You said that during the emergency, about 3.000 to 4.000 volunteers from Serbia joined the TO in the region. What sort of dates are we talking about? Is this 1991 or earlier or later?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The period -- well, I was referring to, and I hope Mr. Milosevic was referring to that too, because that's when volunteers were necessary -- August 1991 to November/December 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, if you say -- if you've given us that time frame, from August to December 1991, were those then members of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Members of the JNA were a different category with their reserve units and Territorial Defence. That was different. And they were equipped in Serbia and would arrive --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The JNA was equipped in Yugoslavia, because it was the Yugoslav People's Army; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But these volunteers, weren't they -- the ones you're talking about, weren't they members of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already answered that. Those members, those 3.000 to 4.000 men, were with the Territorial Defence of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. That's one thing, one lot. The other lot are reservists and volunteers who came from the Yugoslav People's Army and there were 36.000 of them approximately in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mean JNA troops?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On the territory of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not on the territory of Yugoslavia. On the territory of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, wasn't that Yugoslav territory in 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. But we didn't use that term up till now. We always referred to the forces of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But in 1991, de facto and de jure, that was the territory of Yugoslavia

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, up until the recognition of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And that took place in 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And after the recognition of Croatia, there were no war operations on that territory, were there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some sporadic return fire, but I don't think it could be termed "war operations."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So the answer is no, there were no war operations in that territory then. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said there were none.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You say in paragraph 21 that you don't know the reasons for which Radovan Stojicic, Badza, went from Slavonia to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that he did travel to Belgrade, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you don't know the reasons. Well, don't you know that he lived in Belgrade, resided in Belgrade, he had a family in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know that. I would sometimes accompany him. Sometimes he would go to see his children, and at others he would go to attend working meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you had a personal friendly relationship with him, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So because of this friendly, personal relationship, the conviction prevailed that you were some sort of link and connection between the MUP of Serbia and Slavonia; isn't that right? And you actually say that in paragraph 23.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once Badza had left the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And were you a link between the MUP of Serbia and Slavonia, or due to circumstances was that ascribed because of your friendship with him, ascribed to you because of your friendship with him?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'd say both.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then you go on to explain that your contacts with Radovan Stojicic continued to be friendly and on a personal footing when he went to take up his new position. You would often go to see him in Belgrade, you say. And you also say that you informed him about the situation in the Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem district. So he didn't have any sources about the situation but relied on you to inform him; is that it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he learnt about it from me, but firstly he was a policeman and they use a number of sources for their information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So your personal relationship, that is, between you and him, was not the relationship of a MUP and the Republic of Srpska Krajina or Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. You had personal ties, a personal relationship, the two of you; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've already answered a similar question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Now, you say that in the course of 1991 in Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, that there was a unit of the MUP of Serbia. And that is in paragraph 28 of your statement. And you say that it numbered approximately 100 men. Is it true that -- and in command of the unit, as you say, was Veljko Bogunovic. I can see that from these statements of yours. Is it true that this man Bogunovic and his unit was exclusively composed of policemen from the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was entirely made up of policemen from the Republic of Croatia who had been dismissed in the Republic of Croatia or had tendered their resignation, didn't want to work under the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. All right. Fine.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a minute, please. I haven't completed my answer. And they were all given work as -- in the MUP of Serbia and as members of the MUP of Serbia. They came to Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Where did you get this other piece of information from, policemen who were dismissed set up a unit which in the territory of the republic they had been worked up until then suddenly became employees of the MUP of Serbia? Where do you get that information from?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is no idea of mine. It's an exact piece of information, because 99 per cent of those people still work in the MUP of Serbia today.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Where professional policemen found professional employ and where they're working today has nothing to do with the fact that they were policemen working in Croatia; is that right? This man Bogunovic, was he from Croatia as well?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you can check that out on the basis of his work booklets, employee booklets.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is that man Bogunovic from Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They're all from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I see, all from Croatia. Right. Now, is it true that they were under the command of the Territorial Defence of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem and not under the command of Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When they were in the territory, they were under the command of the commander of the TO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Now, is it true that the police of Serbia - so this whole sector of public security - was never in the territory? It was only after Operation Storm and the chaos that ensued after it that there was one unit which helped have law and order prevail and sort of -- to border security. And there were no operations then either; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A specialist anti-terrorist unit does come under the sector of public security.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It wasn't a special anti-terrorist unit which was deployed in the area, was it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already answered that question, that its commander was there and more than half the members of the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that there was Badza, that you don't know in what capacity he was there, and you said that he was accompanied by about 15 people.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, approximately 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, 15. So Badza with 15 men launched an aggression against Croatia; is that what you're claiming?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. You're misrepresenting the evidence again, and we have already been over this particular issue to a great deal of length. So let's move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please, you mentioned that there was a unit of the MUP of Serbia under the command of Obrad Stevanovic. Could you explain that to me, please.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the fall of Western Slavonia and the lower part of Krajina, sometime in August this unit arrived and it was deployed in the area right up until April 1996, which was when it withdrew. And it was exclusively there to ensure that law and order prevailed, to keep the peace. There were no war operations, but there was an immediate threat of war that was possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, did that unit defend the frontier, the border, and help ensure that law and order prevailed after the chaos following Operation Storm? Is that what it was doing? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So did that unit have any combat operations vis-a-vis anybody at the time there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So, in fact, that unit was there to assist the authorities in the area, to help them see that law and order prevailed, and to help them in matters of traffic control and fighting crime as well. Is that what it was doing there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my assessment, that view -- that unit had the greatest role to play by supplying moral support to the people in Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's not pursue the point about this unit, because you yourself say there was no -- no combat operations. But tell me this now, please: You mentioned the demilitarisation plan and the transformation of the 11th Corps. Now, tell me, is it true that the plan for the demilitarisation and transformation of the 11th Corps was compiled in 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The corps was set up sometime in 1993 and 1994 whereas the plan for demilitarisation of the 11th Corps was completed immediately after the signing of the Erdut Agreement, in the spirit of the agreement's implementation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You have provided here a text of the Erdut Agreement but only in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. It's tab 27 of Exhibit 549, for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then we can see that it was signed by you and Hrvoje Sarinic, and that the others, Galbraith and Stoltenberg, were participants in the peace process. Did this agreement ensure the halting of violence and the exodus of Serbs from Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The agreement guaranteed a peaceful solution, a peaceful settlement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I draw your attention to point 12. There were two years of a transitional period during which when everything settles down people could decide how they would organise their lives. No one had to decide anything in haste. The period envisaged was one year plus another year. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Even General Loncar, who was commander of the 11th Corps, remained as some sort of - I don't know how to put it - assistant to the international administrator, Walker, at the time in Eastern Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, General Loncar did remain for a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now I should like to draw your attention to point 12, which envisages -- unfortunately, I only have it in English, so I'll read it out in English, but it will be translated for you. [In English] "Not later than 30 days before the end of the transitional period" --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: "elections for all local government bodies, including for municipalities, districts, and counties, as well as the right of the Serbian community to appoint a joint Council --" [Interpretation] I'm not getting a translation. Is this being translated? Are you hearing the translation?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Could I hear the B/C/S translation, please.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not getting it either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: There's no interpretation from English into Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's try again.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So I'm reading point 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: "Not later than 30 days before the end of the transitional period, elections for all local government bodies, including for municipalities, districts, and counties, as well as the right of the Serbian community to appoint a joint Council of municipalities, shall be organised by the Transitional Administration," [Interpretation] et cetera. So this agreement establishes the right of the Serbs to organise a joint council of municipalities, because it says "right of the Serbian community to appoint a joint Council of municipalities." Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What I'm trying to say is did this provide for a peaceful settlement for all and did it envisage the right of the Serb community to form a joint council of municipalities in the area?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is common knowledge. Only I don't know whether it was actually formed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was a joint council of municipalities formed?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that no longer exists in Croatia. I think it's now called a "zupanja" or county.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So this is -- the practice nowadays does not conform with that Erdut Agreement. So the Serbs no longer have the right to this joint council of municipalities, though it was provided for by the Erdut Agreement.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they don't, unless the "zupanja" means that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The "zupanja" certainly doesn't mean that, because this joint council of municipalities is envisaged as the right of the Serbian community.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this did not come into being, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That was not the only agreement that was not complied with, but let us move on. You say that you had a direct connection -- I have to tell you that I hear this for the first time, and I find it hard to believe, but you'll probably be able to explain this to me -- that you were -- had a direct line with Milan Milutinovic. With me you never had a direct line, but you apparently had one with Milan Milutinovic. Will you please explain this to me. You had a telephone line? Milan Milutinovic at the time was the minister for foreign affairs, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean telephone line?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. No, in paragraph 30, you refer to a telephone line.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said in my statement, I had a telephone starting with the numbers 025, which means the Sombor municipality. Then I had the 011 for Belgrade --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, if you call Belgrade from here, you also have to dial 011.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We must bring this to a close for the moment. It's -- it's time now for an adjournment. We can come back to it after the adjournment. We'll adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you've got -- you have an hour and three-quarters left. You've had over two hours with this witness. The Prosecution had just over three hours. It's right you should have a bit longer because of the statement too. So three hours and three-quarters in all, which means you've got an hour and three-quarters left. Mr. Milanovic, I interrupted you, I think, when you were -- you were going to say something. But it may be that we can get back to it through -- is there anything you'd like to add? Wait a minute. Wait a minute.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hadn't answered the question. In addition to these two telephones from the Republic of Serbia, I had a phone that was known as a special line, with four digits, and it was only the government of Serbia, the MUP, the army, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the public security, the state security, and some other ministries had this number. So I was able to contact directly Milan Milutinovic and others who had these numbers and they could contact me and no one else could do so.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, may we first clear up this question of time. You admitted this witness under the new Rule 89, and there's a large quantity of documents that have been tendered without any examination-in-chief. So I think that an hour and three-quarters that you are giving me is insufficient for me to complete the cross-examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It bears all that in mind. It also bears in mind the length of time which you'll have vis-a-vis the Prosecution. Yes, let's go on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is precisely why I'm asking you to reconsider this once again, because Madam Uertz-Retzlaff tendered most of the documents without any examination, as you know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: All right. Well, now is your opportunity, if you want, if it's necessary to look at these documents. It may be not be necessary, but if you want to, now is your opportunity. But you've got an hour and three-quarters left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milanovic, tell me, where did you get the idea that Radovan Stojicic was outside the chain of command of the MUP when he was in the MUP? He was assistant minister. How could he be outside the MUP chain of command when he was assistant minister in the MUP? I'm talking about the time when he was the assistant minister and not about the time when he was a volunteer in your area.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I came to the conclusion that Minister Sokolovic left everything related to public and state security to his assistants and that he did not interfere much into their work, that they mostly made their decisions themselves, and I do know that very frequently he would stay at home, without even coming to work every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you claiming that Minister Zoran Sokolovic was not performing his duty but that his assistants for the public and state security worked without his approval and without his approval and without discussions at the senior level meetings?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that, but I said that they had a free hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On what ground did you come to that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Radovan Stojicic himself told me that several times, and I saw when decisions were being taken that when you call up on the phone you omit the proper level in the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in most cases the three of them came to see me, that is, the minister and the two assistants, heads of the two departments?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't doubt that, but they certainly must have come individually too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is this something you're saying on the basis of an impression that you gained?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let's move on to the next topic. You testified about a Skorpions unit which was led by Slobodan Medic. Where were they from? Are they from your area?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you engage them?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you engage them in your area?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the area is concerned, I proposed, as is stated in this text, in my statement, I proposed to the director of the oil company that they secure the oil fields that were on the separation lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that you personally found them, rallied them, organised them, and engaged them privately to protect the oil fields?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, who engaged them, then, to defend the oil fields in your area?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I proposed Slobodan Medic as the person who should be in charge of that security, and then they were under the director of the oil company.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So this was a security unit for the oil company, the head of which you yourself proposed.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Why did it happen that you chose Medic to be at the head of the security detail in the oil company in your area?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Having toured the area, I realised that the oil fields were in jeopardy as they were along the very confrontation line. And it is common knowledge that if a shell were to fall, this would cause an ecological disaster. I toured the area. I met this young man for the first time. He was proposed to me by several people. And I even remember that I asked Badza even whether he had anything against this, and he said he didn't. This young man was about 22 or 23 years old at the time, and he organised the task well and continued working at it until the end of 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you also sent them to Bosnia and Herzegovina, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't send them. The command of the corps sent them to accomplish various assignments, and most of those units that went outside the area I would visit very frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, as deputy defence minister, I assume you had a decisive say. As you appointed Medic yourself, you would decide where you would send him.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you know yourself, according to the law on defence, the ministry does not have the right to order the engagement of the army. This is a right vested in the government and the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. So the government sent them.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the government and the army command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did you mention that when the bombing of Yugoslavia started by NATO forces, that you sent him to Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned that after the NATO attack on the Federal Republic, seven, eight, or ten days after that he called me up and told me that he'd rather not go as a reservist to the army of Yugoslavia but as a member of MUP. At the same time - and I didn't mention this - I was called up by General Djordjevic, the head of the public security, saying that he needed volunteers. So I didn't know what to do for three or four days, whether to send him or not, because everything was being monitored. I didn't know whether I should get in touch with the two of them, and three or four days later I did establish -- link the two of them up, and two or three days later he went to Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was he returned from there following General Djordjevic's orders? He demanded that he return?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was returned, but he went back and stayed until the end of the bombing raids.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that when General Vasiljevic testified here it was mentioned that he and this group of his committed various crimes in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what General Vasiljevic said, but I do know that two of his men were suspects and that proceedings are underway in Yugoslavia, that is, in Serbia. Now, the trial will show what is right and what isn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that Vasiljevic testified against me, even though he did so, he said that I insisted that whoever committed a crime had to be held accountable and they mentioned him?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness really can't deal with this. He wasn't here. It's somebody else's evidence. He can't comment on that. Yes, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Is it you that Vlastimir Djordjevic never came to your area officially?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: True.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You frequently mention the Vance Owen Plan. In the examination-in-chief and since that, it's not the Vance Owen Plan, it's the Vance Plan. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Isn't it true that the army of Yugoslavia in conformity with that plan withdrew its units from the territory of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in April or May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Doesn't this unequivocally show that the JNA advocated a peaceful settlement to the Yugoslav crisis as a whole?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's not for the witness to say. That's a matter of comment, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Do you remember that Milan Babic, who at the time was at the head of the Republic of Srpska Krajina, refused to accept Vance's plan and that that is precisely why on the 8th of January, 1992 I sent a public letter, an open letter to Babic, explaining my positions?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that you did prevail upon the leadership in the lower part of Krajina to have them accept the Vance Plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And is it true and correct that in -- despite the fact that Croatia accepted the Security Council decision itself linked to the Krajina area for the Vance Peace Plan to be applied there, that is to say, to be -- UN-protected areas to be proclaimed, that they did not respect that because in mid-June 1992 they stormed the Miljevac plateau and committed great crimes against the Serbs on that occasion? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember that they violated the Vance Plan for the lower part of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That was in June 1992. Now, do you remember that already at the beginning of 1993 there was an attack on Ravni Kotelar [phoen], the Maslenicki Bridge, Perica [phoen], Zemunik, where several hundred Serbs were killed and several hundred more wounded?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then in October 1993, once again an attack on the Medak pocket area, when once again Serb settlements were destroyed and a large number of Serbs massacred? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, I am enumerating the key and greatest crimes committed at the time. Now, is it also true, on the other hand, that after the arrival of the UN the Serbs from Krajina never entered territory under the control of Croatia, never stormed the territory under the control of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's also true, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did Krajina have its Ministry of the Interior? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did it have its state security? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it also correct that Krajina had its own Red Berets, which were called the Red Berets of Krajina? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not quite sure about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You don't know?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness has said he's not sure about it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As you mentioned various people from the Ministry of the Interior, is it true that you knew Jovica Stanisic only superficially, that you only saw him a couple of times in your life?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. During the events that we're talking about. But after that, we would see each other very frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean by "after that"? When is this after period?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me be precise. In 1992, 1993, 1994, rarely. In 1995, a little more often. And also a few times in 1996. Not in 1997. But since -- after his replacement, for about two years, practically every second or third day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you in fact saw him after the war; is that it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what I said. Before and after; mostly after.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, can you give us the names of somebody from the state security of Serbia who came to Krajina during all these war years? Can you give us a name? What are you reading from, if I might inquire?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just to remind myself about 19 -- about paragraph 76 of my statement. For example, out of these 15 or so, quite certainly 70 per cent of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What? 70 per cent of the 15 what?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That they arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What you mean to say is that ten of them, about ten of them came?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, roughly. But they were in the area, and I don't know the exact number. It wouldn't be state security if everyone were to know the exact number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, I see. All right, then. Now, what were they doing in that territory anyway?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that they were going about their business.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mean collecting intelligence? Is that it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did they take part in any combat operations? Do you know that any of them committed any crimes perhaps?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As to crimes, I don't know about that. But rumour had it -- now, as I wasn't active in 1991 -- rumour had it that some individuals did take part in the fighting. But I never heard of them committing any crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You have presented certain accusations against certain individuals. You mention Dusan Orlovic, and say he worked in the state security of Serbia. Is it, however, true that that man actually worked in the Ministry of the Internal Affairs of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is an example in point, that somebody is working like him in Krajina and in the DB of Serbia, and I have exact information that he's still working in the DB of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As to today, I'm not interested in that. I'm interested in those times. Was he in the executive government of Krajina at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was, as an employee of the DB of Serbia at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you mean he was a member of the executive authorities of Krajina in the capacity of a DB of Serbia employee?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was employed in both ministries.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How was that possible? How could he have been employed by both ministries?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there you have it. It is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You say that you attended meetings with Stanisic and that he asked you about the situation in Slavonia and it was peaceful the whole time when you communicated with him. There were no combat operations at the time.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was a time of peace, and the Blue Helmets would either be arriving or there was demilitarisation afoot, that kind of thing, everything linked to security.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, if they had their men there, why would he have to ask you whether you -- if they had information from the source, why would he have to ask you about the situation, if he could get it from the source?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said; he liked several sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You go on to say that after the 5th of August, 1995 a certain man called Momir Gavrilovic, Gavra, an operative of the DB, was sent and he introduced himself falsely as Colonel Milan Peric, gave false identity. Now, tell me, was there a crime that had been committed in the region or what was he doing there in the first place? Was he doing something that was not allowed? Did anything actually happen, or did you just think that up, invent it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't invent anything. No crime took place. The fact of it was that the man was present and he was chief of security of the 11th Corps. And it is you who invented the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I'm just asking on the basis of what it says -- what you yourself state.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there's nothing there about a crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm asking you, because you're testifying here, whether a crime had been perpetrated or not. From what you wrote, it would emerge that you increased salary and funds and resources from the budget without the region knowing, and then you mentioned Belje, NIK, Vinarija and some other companies; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In agreement with the representatives of the authorities of the Srem-Baranja region, that's what we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you did not coordinate that with the government in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we bypassed Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, did you know that Yugoslavia offered humanitarian assistance to the budget of Srpska Krajina to finance social welfare, health welfare, education, and things of that kind?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know that money came from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and that it filled the coffers of our budget for the purposes which you mentioned. Mostly it was spent on the army and police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I have a piece of information here from the 1st of December, 1993, for example, resources for the army in your budget were 43.65, and they were covered by credits issued by the national bank of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. And I assume you ought to know that; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that exactly, but I do know that in different way the budget was covered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, is it true that these high credits with the national bank of the Republic of Serbian Krajina was possible precisely because of the production and processing of crude oil precisely in your region? Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly, because that was one of the largest sources of revenue for the budget of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in 1991 and 1992 organs -- the organs of Croatia interrupted the payments from -- coming in and out of the Krajina region and that all of you had to have this turnover amongst yourselves and via the accounts you opened in Yugoslavia? Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Srem and Baranja region, this interruption began in August and September. Nothing more was being done, with Croatia, that is, no business dealings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the payments -- payments, transactions that you had with the SDK or social accounting service in Yugoslavia, that was based on an agreement signed for providing services for payments of various kinds with the branch offices in Novi Belgrade and Sombor; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I'm well acquainted with this area, but probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the Republic of Serbian Krajina set up its own service of payments and organised branch offices for payments in Knin, Petrinja, Vukovar, Beli Manastir, and so on, in order to be able to deal with the flow of money, to allow the economy to function and the public services to function?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did. And I think that was in 1992, but I can't remember the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, in October 1992, is it true that the budget of the Republic of Serbian Krajina was established and put into effect, that it was formed in the organs of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, in actual fact?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably it was, but I don't remember the exact period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you do remember that in the course of 1992 assistance from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia for social welfare, health, education, and so on, for pensioners was ensured? There were 20.000 pensioners in Krajina and former fighters, they had invalidity payments?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, assistance was frequently sought and received.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: There were 50.000 pensioners who had realised their rights by paying into the pension fund of Croatia and received nothing from it; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were cases of that kind, quite a lot of them, but I don't know the exact number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia okayed humanitarian aid in 1992 amounted to 930 million dinars, and that was just 5 per cent of the resources and revenue from the budget to the end of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember those figures.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As this comes under your realm of activity, do you remember how much oil production there was, how much oil was produced in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say exactly for 1992, but I think on an average it was 250 tonnes, from 1992 to 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: 250 tonnes per day?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, per day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me this now, please: You've been speaking about the relationship between Goran Hadzic and myself. First of all, you don't know about our relationship firsthand, do you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you would make comments from time to time when we were together.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you said here that you came to see me for the first time in 1993 or 1994; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember exactly, but roughly thereabouts. Perhaps a little before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But I assume you know that I'd got to know Goran Hadzic when he was president of the region. How could I know -- have known him before that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He can't -- he can't answer that. The witness can't answer that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the witness has already answered, because he said that he came to see me first in 1993 and 1994. I assume some dates can be compared.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But tell me this. I didn't quite follow what was said. You said something about Perisic and the presence of the army along the Danube. You mean the presence of the army at the Danube on our side of the Danube? Is that it? Is that what you meant?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as it says in the statement. If you want me to explain, I'll be happy to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I wanted you to explain the presence of our army along the Danube on our territory. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The army was along -- whether they were called border units or front units. Anyway, Perisic at one point withdrew them to the depth, to the rear. They weren't along the border itself. And then had them returned there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But let's take all this together. And as you say, what has that got to do with whether they were further up front or further behind? I don't suppose you challenge the fact that that army was on the territory of Yugoslavia, whichever the variation and whatever the position, further forward or further back?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't see what there is to challenge there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the army was on Yugoslav territory, not on the territory of your region.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said that the foremost detachment was up at the border itself, the frontier, but on its -- in its own state.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I just wanted to clarify that point.
