And when you mention a press conference in Erdut, you talk about the people present and then mention a certain Major Suco, or something like that. You mention this Major Suco, a colonel or "puki", "pukovnik puki", a retired general. So he was an active -- he was not an active JNA officer, was he? That's not in dispute.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The investigator Dzuro showed me a tape, and I recognised some people on it, and among those people was this man, and he was a pensioner. He was retired. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. In paragraph 40 you mention that Badza in your friend's apartment, Zavisic, in Novi Sad accused you of supporting Goran Hadzic. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to explain that. He invited me to this apartment and he accused me for the failure of the first round of the elections in the Republic of Serbian Krajina, because Martic got few votes in Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, that I shouldn't have undermined his position and to join forces with Goran but that I should have supported Martic and that now in the second round I should support Martic, because for the second round only he and Babic remained.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, why would he accuse you of supporting Goran Hadzic when previously you said that Hadzic was some sort of -- my man? Why, then, would Badza accuse you of supporting Hadzic when Badza was my associate? He was deputy minister of the interior.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you should remember that at that time my position was that neither Martic nor Hadzic nor Babic should be supported but that we should find someone else from our sleeves who would be able to bear the burden of the politics that were ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did you know that the leadership of Serbia was on poor terms with Babic, to put it briefly, because he acted in an extreme manner and he was opposed to any kind of negotiations and a peaceful settlement?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that, but that was poor strategy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the leadership of Serbia advocated and supported people who were in favour of a peaceful solution and negotiations?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometimes it was like that and sometimes it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it is far for me to make any conclusion on the basis of this answer of yours. Whenever you mention a meeting that you attended and you were attending as a member of a delegation, so you were not leading that delegation, and there were always -- there was always talk of negotiations and efforts to reach a peaceful settlement.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll give you an example. You yourself said that you supported Goran Hadzic, as far as I understood you, and even if you didn't say it that is what I'm claiming.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you chose him, not me. Who chose Goran Hadzic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know that he was against the signing of the Erdut Agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The Erdut Agreement came later.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well. So sometimes support and sometimes not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The Erdut Agreement came in 1995. This has nothing to do with this. Surely you know that I met Goran Hadzic when he was president already and when he came officially to visit Serbia to seek assistance and who wanted to talk. So I couldn't have influenced his promotion because he already had reached the highest level he could have over there when I met him. Surely you know that.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to what Goran said, it wasn't so. Goran would say that he often went to see you as president of the National Council and not of the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. In any event, he was the number-one man in the area when he came to see me; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let's not dwell on that any further. You say in paragraph 40 that telephone lines - and please explain this to me - between Serbia and Slavonia were interrupted because you didn't wish to support Martic and that they were re-established when you finally agreed to support Martic, and that Martic was elected thanks to you. That is what one gathers from what you say. Is that possible?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't put it in those terms, but that I did assist, you know that very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you saying that you lobbied for Martic as in any elections some people lobby for some and others for others?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the second round, at the request of Badza. Now, how great my role was, I cannot judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, explain to me this point about telephone lines. You say that if you dialled 011, you could contact Belgrade. Surely you know if you're dialling Belgrade from here, you first dial the country number and then 011. What is that -- what is the point you're making? The same applies if you're calling from Belgrade. You have to dial 381-11, you get Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I explained it once, and I'll do it again briefly. Throughout the area of Srem and Baranja, there were only two telephone numbers with the code of Belgrade and a special telephone that I've already explained. And when I do not do as I'm told or if Martic criticises me in Belgrade, then I -- the line is broken and I can't re-establish the line until things calm down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And who installed those lines for you in the first place?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The PTT, in cooperation with the MUP of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the MUP would switch you off when you disagreed with Martic and switch you on when you agreed with Martic; is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's one example.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please: Here in paragraph 82, since this is something we didn't see but you reviewed this in the office of this opposite side, the video footage and those allegedly intercepted conversations, since those exhibits are not being produced here but in the offices of the side opposite, you say in paragraph 82, "The video footage shows the news conference held immediately after the review of the unit. I recognise the following people from this news conference." And then you mention: "Colonel Mladenovic, commander of the Baranja Brigade; Bijorcevic, commander of the Novi Sad Corps; a woman who was secretary of the Beli Manastir Municipal Council, whose name I cannot remember; Zeljko Raznjatovic, known as Arkan; Boro Ivanovic, known as Konj; and Milan Milanovic, known as Mrgud." That's you, isn't it? And then in addition to them, you mention some others. Tell me, what is the significance of this review and what was the role of the JNA and when was this review?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The review occurred just before the pullout of the Yugoslav People's Army. The review was carried out by the commander of the Novi Sad Corps, which means General Andrija Bijorcevic. And after that there was a news conference, at which almost all those present spoke. And the rest is indicated here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When I put a question to you, you don't need to tell me or refer me to what is stated here. But I'm asking, was this review prior to the withdrawal of the JNA in accordance with the Vance Plan?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That is why I'm not sure of the significance of this review. According to the agreement, the army withdrew from the area, then there was a review, and after that, they left. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We've said that several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You say that after the withdrawal of the JNA, in each brigade there were three JNA officers. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the JNA withdrew, in accordance with the Vance Plan, the TO Brigades and the command of the TO for Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, as well as for the whole of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, as it was known by then, were abolished and the weapons were placed under the double-key system. However, it was allowed that a couple of officers should remain in each command in plain clothes and who, in cooperation with the UN, that is, with the Blue Helmets, would tour and check the weapons and artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And was that in agreement with the arrangements made under the peace plan? Weapons were placed under a double key, one key held by the TO of the area and the other by the UN? And wasn't this controlled in accordance with the agreement drawn up based on the Vance Plan?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the heavy weapons remained under the double-key system right up until the Croatian forces violated the agreement reached on the basis of the Vance Plan; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Tell me, please, in connection with what you said, that following orders of Milutinovic and Tomic you shut off the pipeline, oil pipeline, what is that about? Briefly.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the Erdut Agreement was signed and the Dayton Accords, sanctions were lifted on the Federal Republic and Milutinovic called me and said that I should go and see Dragan Tomic, and someone advised me to contact Milutinovic - I can't remember who - that I should go to see Dragan Tomic and arrange with him for the oil lines to be closed, that is, for the Krk-Pancevo oil to be stopped so that the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia could import oil from China. I could describe this in greater detail if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Surely you know there was a contract between the FRY and Croatia on the delivery of oil through -- via the terminal at Krk, regardless of where the oil was coming from.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is not in dispute. But for that to be done, we stopped drilling oil from the Srem-Baranja region altogether, and Goran Hadzic and the delegation that went to see you criticised me for this. I hope you remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Probably that was as you say, but I don't remember you being somebody that was attacked by somebody. I really don't know that anyone attacked you.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean in words. I don't mean physically.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, in words. That's what I'm saying. I don't know that somebody criticised you in particular. A series of documents were produced here, but due to the limited time I have I will certainly not have an occasion to go into them in detail. But let's -- let's take a look at least at some of them, some of those that have been referred to in particular during your examination-in-chief. We have here a document, official report of the conversation between the Prime Minister of the RSK government and Slobodan Milosevic, ERN 02077285.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: [Previous translation Continues] ... tab 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Immediately after the first paragraph -- have you found it? I'll be very brief. So please give me a brief answer to a couple of questions related to each document. So in the first paragraph, it says: "From the Republic of Serbia --" it says who was present, "From the Republic of Serbia, the President, Slobodan Milosevic, Prime Minister Radoman Bozovic, and the governor of the National Bank of Serbia." So the Prime Minister, the governor of the national bank, and myself. And then in the second paragraph the topic of discussion is defined, the meeting agreed on the method of extending financial aid to Krajina up until the end of the year. Is it clear that this delegation of Krajina, as can be seen from the composition of those from Serbia, that is, the Prime Minister and the governor of the national bank, apart from me, that this delegation had come to ask for financial aid from Serbia? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's not at issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the topic of discussion is financial aid of Serbia to the Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Fine. Let's go on to the next document. The Republic of Serbian Krajina, Ministry of the Interior, 0207669, sent to the president, that is, to me, to the Prime Minister, to the minister of the interior, and Milan Martic signed it, addressing all of us together, highly unfavourable material and financial situation. Have you found the document?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: That's tab 14, Your Honours, of the same exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Anyway, this is what it says: The highly unfavourable material and financial situation of this ministry finds itself, as well as the Republic of Serbian Krajina, have prompted us to write to you so that within the frameworks of your capabilities you could lend us assistance. And then Milan Martic goes on to ask for financial assistance. Is that at issue or not?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see nothing that would be at issue there. I just testified to the fact that this was an authentic document, that they are indeed the signatures and stamps of those people, and that all that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Now, what is there that is not normal; that is to say, that the Republic of Serbia is offering financial assistance to its own people in Krajina? Anything out of the ordinary there? Anything unlawful or contentious or anything along those lines that could be called into issue for any reason? Could you answer that question, please.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said that the document was authentic and that that was the assistance asked for. It's not up to me to judge whether it is normal, abnormal, out of the ordinary, or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Milanovic. Now, take a look at the next document. And during the examination-in-chief, I did draw attention to that, 0207683 is its number. The heading is "The Republic of Serbian Krajina, the government."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Tab 17?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And they addressed the government of the Republic of Serbia and Montenegro and the governor of the national bank of Yugoslavia. So it is at a Yugoslav level. The competent authorities for monetary questions and republican levels and governments. The subject is request for unity in the credit and monetary system. This is the demand they sent --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Exhibit 352, tab 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And on page 2, the first paragraph states, "From the day the war broke out in the area of the Republika Srpska Krajina, payments transactions were being done via commercial banks in their branch offices from the territory of the Republic of Serbia," which, as we have already noted, according to the agreement was done, put into effect. Now, do you know that a unified credit and monetary system was never established? Do you know that the Republic of Serbian Krajina had its own central bank, in actual fact, and that it had the Krajina dinar, as it was called? Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So what was in use in Krajina was the Krajina dinar, and the central bank of Krajina had all the monetary power and authority; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that the Krajina dinar was minted in Belgrade at the Topcider mint of Belgrade; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that the printing of money is a service and a commercial operation which can be done for foreign countries? Many countries have their money printed elsewhere or minted elsewhere if they don't have the necessary equipment to do so themselves. So do you know that the monetary authority in Krajina was in fact the central bank of Krajina and that the method of payment was the Krajina dinar?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on to something else. Within your realm, that is to say, the army. We have a document here, 0201815, in which the chief of the General Staff of the army of Yugoslavia, Colonel Zivota Panic is issuing an order that through the military districts recruits should be taken in and sent out?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's have the tab number, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Tab 152 of Exhibit 352.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It says here that "With the aim of organising acceptance and initiation of the conscript soldiers who are in the SFRY, I hereby order that they organise the acceptance and initiation of the conscript soldiers who are responding to the appeal of the government of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina, should report to the army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina." You were the assistant defence minister at the time, so in the Republic of Srpska Krajina, after the attack by the Croatian forces, mobilisation was proclaimed, a large number of people and conscripts, as you know, were on the territory of Yugoslavia, the government of the Republic of Serbian Krajina put out a mobilisation, and here the chief of the General Staff is helping to organise the acceptance and accommodation of the people who, at the invitation of the government of Srpska Krajina, should put their name down for going to the Republic of the Serbian Krajina. So the citizens of the Republic of Serbian Krajina who put down their names to go to the army of Serbian Krajina at the invitation of the government of Serbian Krajina should be accepted and accommodated and be enabled to go there.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And what is your question? I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, is -- does this concern the acceptance and accommodation of those who have put up their names to go to the Serbian Krajina, to help with their accommodation and having them go there and nothing more than that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was anybody forced to go to the army there, or is it -- or does it just say those who respond to the call from the government to go there? Isn't that something quite normal? They have responded to the general call.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I testified to the fact that this was an authentic document, judging by the heading, the stamp, and the signature. Now, as far as the issue is concerned, I consider this is normal. But there were rumours going round that some people were forced to mobilise, although I don't have any specific information about that, and this does not refer to the Srem and Baranja region. These were conscripts that went to the lower regions of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, have a look at point 4. This is just acceptance for those who have signed up themselves. And then it says: "The assignments of conscript soldiers shall be performed by the government office of the Republic of Serbian Krajina in Belgrade." There was a bureau, and the address is stated. It is Mosa Pijada Street, number 8, and cooperation must be established with them. And it gives the telephone number. So it is the government office of the Republic of Serbian Krajina who will perform this; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is there any - how shall I put this? - military role on the part of the Yugoslav army with respect to filling the full complement? You were deputy defence minister, so is there anything irregular here or out of order?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't really say what was in order and what wasn't. From this document, we can see that the General Staff of what was already the VJ did help the Republic of Serbian Krajina with respect to mobilising the recruits, the conscripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, conscripts who, at the invitation of the government, sign up to go, that they should organise their acceptance and accommodation and that it is the government office of the Republic of Serbian Krajina in Belgrade which was charged with doing this. So where is the problem there? It would be an embassy in another country that would do so for conscripts signing up. Isn't that logical?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you waiting for an answer? I've already answered your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What was your answer?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer was that this is assistance of the Yugoslav army to the government of the Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it quite clear that there is no coercion here, nobody being forced, forced mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From this document, I cannot see that it is forced mobilisation, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Very well. Let's have a look further down. I've turned the page to the Serb original. It is tab 22 of Exhibit 327. You provided a document here of the Serbian Krajina, the Ministry of the Interior, the offices of the minister, to the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serbia and to Deputy Minister Mr. Radomir Stojicic personally. His name isn't Radomir but Radovan. I'm just -- this just shows how well they know him; they can't even write his name down properly. The date is the 22nd of March, 1995. And it says: "With your help, the Sabotage Squad of the Special Brigade of the RSK MUP is finishing a one-month course with your anti-terrorist units. Could you please continue the training ... of two members of our brigade who carry out permanent brigade duties as instructors/saboteurs. We would add that these are very responsible and conscientious members of the brigade who proved," et cetera, et cetera, "to be reliable fighters and members of our service, especially," et cetera. "We thank you for your understanding," et cetera. So this is a one-month course within the frameworks of the anti-terrorist units -- well, I'm sure you know that our officers during the SFRY were trained in various armed forces in different armies, ranging from America to Russia -- or first of all, from Russia right up to the United States. They were trained there. So what is there strange if somebody sends a group of people to attend a one-month course in some specialty to a friendly fraternal country, for example, for training?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't see anything strange there. But let me repeat once again, all I said was -- was that this was an authentic document, that the heading, stamp, and signature was from Knin, and that -- that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. Let's just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Before we go on, we're going to consider the time position. Just one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're going to give you one hour from now, ten minutes of which you can take up till 2.00 and then you can have 50 minutes tomorrow, and we'll give you some additional time which you've asked for. Yes. So let's go on for another ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Will you please now look at tab 15 of Exhibit 352. It is the 19th of June, 1992, the government of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, Knin, addressed to the Federal Executive Council, which means the government of Yugoslavia, the Federal Secretariat for Finance, and the national bank of Yugoslavia, to the governor and deputy governor personally. And then it says: "Will you please in accordance with Rule -- Article 6 on the Law of Assuring Supplementary Funds in the Federal Budget for Financing Social and other Services in the area of the SFRY, which is under the Special Protection of the United Nations in 1992, please pay the necessary sum of 12.900.000.000 dinars, into the funds of the Budget of the Republika Srpska Krajina no later than the 29th of June, 1992." The giro account number is given, of the Budget of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. Mr. Milanovic, does this document show that the budget of the Federation for financing social and other services in the part of SFRY territory which is under special protection of the United Nations envisages a sum for aid and that the government or Krajina is requesting that this envisaged sum in the budget of Yugoslavia be paid into its account, the account of the budget of the Republic of Serbian Krajina? And this paper shows nothing other than that.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the question is ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the budget is a public document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A public document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the government of Yugoslavia submitted the budget to the National Assembly and that there was an item in the budget to finance Social Services in a part of the territory of SFRY which is under special protect of the United Nations in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We've said several times that the federal state assisted the budget of the Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, what's the problem, then? What does this document mean to you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what it means. I was just shown this exhibit and asked whether I consider it to be authentic. I'm not entering into whether it is correct or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you're not entering into the contents. A whole pile of documents are being produced here which I don't understand the reason why they're being tendered, but that's why I'm asking myself, so what? If the government of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia extends material aid to Krajina, and what then?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You don't have to ask the witness a question about it unless it's of significance.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] None of this is relevant for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- what you are trying to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. That will be a matter for us to determine. But meanwhile, why don't you move on and try and finish your cross-examination earlier.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a few more documents, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Look now at another document from the Ministry of the Interior, the administration for public security, tab 19 of 352. This is also produced as an exhibit. Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serbian, the administration for frontier affairs, Belgrade, and it says, "On the 8th of November, 1993, at the frontier crossing Raca two workers will enter the Republic of Serbia from the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serbian Krajina to escort money from Belgrade to Knin." And then it gives the names of those workers - and I won't read them - and the license plate -- registration numbers of the pistols carried by those workers as official pistols, what vehicles they are using, what is the license plate of that vehicle, that they be allowed entry and exit from the Republic of Serbia. So this is something that would apply under normal procedure in any other country as well. An indication is given as to who these people are, data about them, registration numbers, license plates, with the indication that they are escorting the money. Is there anything here that you could describe as illegal, abnormal, or out of the ordinary?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This was the regular practice when crossing the border.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was it the normal practice 20 years before that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But it is the normal practice today, if you're asking another country for somebody to enter it under arms, if he's escorting somebody or something. What other practice can there be?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as another state is concerned, yes. But I'm -- I thought that you were asking me whether that was the regular procedure in these areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is there anything unusual there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I say for the third time that I see nothing unusual or out of the ordinary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The national bank of the Republic of Serbian Krajina - that is, tab 18 of Exhibit 352 - it's addressed to the national bank of Yugoslavia. Request for cash grant. "Please, for the needs of the National Bank of the Republic of Serbian Krajina grant a new amount totalling to 10 billion dinars [as interpreted]. "Since we're nearing the end of July, and the deadline for paying members of the army, police pensions, et cetera, our needs for cash are great. In order for the National Bank of the Republic Serbian Krajina to provide the funds necessary to cover the requirements cited, it needs in addition to the cash it has in its own treasury another 10 billion dinars [as interpreted]. Regards, Governor Pavao, Marjanovic." So cash, when people talk about cash here, that is in our language "gotovina". The earnings of public servants were paid out in cash, weren't they? There was no system of cards, cheques, et cetera. If any, it was extremely limited. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Everything was done in cash. And I don't think any -- I don't see anything at issue here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did most employees in Yugoslavia receive their salaries in cash?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In those days, I think they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And even before those times, they most frequently received their salaries in cash. Few received them through cheques. Mr. Milanovic, I'm asking you to clarify this because a question is frequently raised here as to the transfer of cash from Yugoslavia. And now we see that quite legally with an attachment of the national bank of Yugoslavia cash is being carried to Knin as a subsidy to the national bank of the Republic of Serbian Krajina and in cash. You were a deputy minister. Isn't this a completely legal transaction based on the law?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, I think it was legal. And mostly during that wartime period and under conditions of very high inflation, throughout the territory of the former republics and Krajina, cash was used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. It's 2.00. We'll adjourn now. Fifty minutes left, Mr. Milosevic. We'll adjourn now until 9.00 tomorrow morning. Mr. Milanovic, would you be back then, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: 2.02 p.m., to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 15th of October, 2003 at 9.00 a.m.
